facts.text: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer that sodium ions (Na⁺) and potassium ions (K⁺) cannot cross on their own; they cross only through proteins in it, such as channels and pumps. Sodium is much more concentrated in the extracellular fluid outside the cell than in the cytoplasm, and potassium is much more concentrated in the cytoplasm than outside; each difference is a concentration gradient. All the time, some sodium leaks into the cell and some potassium leaks out through channels, moving down their gradients by diffusion, which needs no energy, the way a drop of food colouring spreads through water from where it is concentrated to where it is not. Left alone, these leaks would run the gradients down. Moving ions the other way, against their gradients from low to high concentration, takes energy, so the sodium-potassium pump, a protein that spans the membrane, carries out active transport.

The sodium-potassium pump, also called Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, works in a repeating cycle. Open toward the cytoplasm, it binds three sodium ions. It then splits one ATP into ADP and phosphate, and the phosphate attaches to the pump; this phosphorylation changes the pump's shape so that it opens toward the extracellular fluid and releases the three sodium ions outside. Open to the outside, it binds two potassium ions from the extracellular fluid. Releasing the phosphate returns the pump to its first shape, open toward the cytoplasm, and it releases the two potassium ions inside. So each cycle spends one ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, both against their concentration gradients, and then the cycle repeats. The pump trades three for two, not one for one.

The pump works like the pumps that fill a town's water tower: they spend electricity to lift water up and store it in the tank, so that water rushes down the moment any faucet opens; the sodium-potassium pump spends ATP to pile sodium up outside the cell, so that sodium rushes in the moment a sodium channel opens. Because the pump moves three positive charges out for every two it brings in, and mainly because potassium leaks out through potassium channels down its gradient, the inside of the cell is negative compared with the outside: the resting membrane potential, about −70 millivolts in a typical neuron. When a neuron is stimulated, sodium channels open and sodium rushes in, down its concentration gradient and toward the negative inside, with no ATP spent: this starts an action potential, the nerve signal that travels along neurons, including those in the brain and spinal cord; in muscle cells, including heart muscle, action potentials trigger contraction. The pump does not make the signal itself: it builds the gradients beforehand and keeps them up over time, and the signal runs on them. The sodium gradient also powers other transport: in the small intestine, cells use sodium flowing in to bring glucose in with it.

Some poisons and drugs bind the sodium-potassium pump and block or slow it. Ouabain, a plant toxin that has been used as an arrow poison, binds the pump on its outer side and blocks it. If the pump is blocked, sodium keeps leaking in and potassium keeps leaking out, so both concentration gradients run down; the resting membrane potential shrinks toward zero, so nerve and muscle cells can no longer fire action potentials normally; and because water follows the sodium into the cell by osmosis, the cell swells and can burst. Digoxin, a heart medicine that comes from the foxglove plant, slows the pump in heart muscle cells; this leads to more calcium inside them, so the heart muscle contracts more strongly.

misconception: Many students think the sodium-potassium pump makes the nerve signal itself. It doesn't: the signal is sodium rushing in through opened sodium channels, downhill and with no ATP spent, using the gradient the pump built beforehand.

lesson_markdown:
# The Sodium-Potassium Pump

**How can a nerve cell fire a signal the instant it's stimulated?**

It stores the energy ahead of time. Spending ATP, the sodium-potassium pump pushes three sodium out and two potassium in, building gradients that power nerve signals.

## Think of a water tower

A town's water tower is filled by pumps that spend electricity lifting water up, so water rushes down the moment any faucet opens. Your cells work the same way: the pump spends ATP piling sodium up outside the cell, so sodium rushes in the moment a sodium channel opens.

## Why the pump has to keep working

1. **The gradients leak.** Sodium is far more concentrated in the extracellular fluid, and potassium is far more concentrated in the cytoplasm; each difference is a **concentration gradient**. Ions can't cross the cell membrane on their own, but a little sodium leaks in and a little potassium leaks out through channels, all the time.
2. **Leaking is downhill; fixing it is uphill.** The leaks are diffusion, like food colouring spreading through water, and need no energy. Pushing ions back against their gradients takes energy, so the pump does **active transport**.
3. **ATP changes the pump's shape.** Open toward the cytoplasm, the pump binds three sodium ions and splits one **ATP**. The phosphate attaches to the pump and flips it open to the outside, where it releases the sodium. It then binds two potassium ions, lets go of the phosphate, flips back and releases the potassium inside.

**Predict:** if three positive charges leave for every two that come in, what happens to the charge inside the cell?

It turns negative. Potassium leaking out through **potassium channels** is actually the main cause, and the three-for-two swap adds to it. The result is the **resting membrane potential**, about −70 millivolts in a typical neuron. (This is simplified: we are leaving out the other ions in the cell.)

## Spending the stored energy

When a neuron is stimulated, **sodium channels** open and sodium rushes in, down its gradient and toward the negative inside, with no ATP spent. That rush starts an **action potential**, the signal that travels along neurons. In muscle cells, including heart muscle, action potentials trigger contraction. The same sodium gradient also helps cells in the small intestine bring in glucose.

| | Sodium-potassium pump | Sodium channel during a signal |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Against the gradient (uphill) | Down the gradient (downhill) |
| Energy | One ATP per cycle | No ATP |
| Job | Builds the gradients ahead of time | Lets sodium in to start the action potential |

## A common mistake

Many students think the pump makes the nerve signal. It doesn't: the signal is sodium flowing downhill through open sodium channels, and the pump's job is building the gradients beforehand and keeping them up over time.

## When the pump stops

Ouabain, a plant toxin that has been used as an arrow poison, blocks the pump. Sodium keeps leaking in and potassium keeps leaking out, so both gradients run down. The resting membrane potential shrinks toward zero, and nerve and muscle cells can no longer fire action potentials normally. Water follows the sodium in, so the cell swells and can burst. Digoxin, a heart medicine from the foxglove plant, slows the pump in heart muscle, so the heart contracts more strongly.

**Check yourself:** An action potential spends no ATP, so why does a cell with a blocked pump eventually stop firing them?

Got a follow-up question? Ask away.
